messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: hiararchical modeling in stan
parts:
Hi,

I have a simple three level hierarchical model to estimate variability: analytical, intra- and inter-lot.

-I wonder if there are ways to speed up the model.
-Is there any regular way to impose priors? For example it is natural to assume that analytical variability is the same for different products so once I have estimated analytical variability for product A I would like to use it as a prior for product B instead of using uninformative prior.

Thanks,
Linas

stan model is attached. It is from pharma domain but I assume similar approach could be used in any manufacturing domain.

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: hiararchical modeling in stan
parts: Whether analytical variability is stable is a domain specific question typically answered by running standard samples on a regular basis, though that is instrument dependent.  For a first pass I would assume yes, I might ask for measurements of standards for a second pass and model it, but always include model checks on that assumption. Depending on the instrument or assay  calibration can be a beast and not everyone understands the role it plays or wants to do it on the suggested schedule. Krzysztof

parts:
On Thursday, August 11, 2016 at 2:03:44 PM UTC-4, Linas Mockus wrote:
The problem is very simple. We have bunch of tablets from different lots and we need to estimate analytical variability, intra- and inter-lot variability. Each tablet is grinded and 3 HPLC injections are run. Assuming that three HPLC injections per tablet are enough to estimate analytical variability the code tries to estimate all three variabilities. Of course I assume that analyst is the same and there is no analyst introduced variability as well as there is no standard variability.

As soon as you say HPLC I don't think you can claim "simple" any more! :)   So it looks like your model is working with concentrations as data rather than the actual response from the HPLC.  In that case I think what you're doing is the best you can do.  Three injections is better than one but you'll still need to assume the analytical variability doesn't change to get enough data to estimate it.  If you were interested in testing that assumption my first guess at an improved model would be to model variability as changing with time as one of the issues with chromatographic instruments is that the response drifts over time (both noise and mean) which is why if you really want to trust your numbers you would run standards, sample, sample, sample, standard, sample, samples, standard, etc... and the model would work with two types of data: a) standards where both the concentration and response are known; and b) samples where only repeated measurements of response are known.  There was a model like that on the list a while back based on one of Andrew's papers but it was challenging IIRC.

Krzysztof

Thanks,
Linas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] hiararchical modeling in stan
parts:
In terms of speed, rather than:

for (i in 1 : N) {
mu [i] <- MU + sigma_intra * ii [lot_samples [i]] + sigma_inter * iii [lots [i]];
log_lik [i] <- normal_log (injections [i], mu [i], sigma);
}
...
increment_log_prob (sum (log_lik));

you can just drop the transformed parameters block altogether and use

injections ~ normal(MU + sigma_intra * ii[lot_samples] + sigma_inter * iii[lots],
sigma);

You'll have to redefine ii and iii as vector[N_LOTS] and vector[N_LOT_SAMPLES]
respectively to allow the vector algebra.

We've also updated the syntax with Stan 2.9, so it's

target += foo;

rather than

increment_log_prob(foo)

and = instead of <- in assignments. We still support the old syntax,
but you'll get deprecation warnings.

- Bob

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] hiararchical modeling in stan
parts:
On Friday, August 12, 2016 at 10:30:35 AM UTC-4, Linas Mockus wrote:
Should I use a more complicated model for measurement error of peak area than just normal? What about the model between concentration and peak area? Should it be linear or some other shape?

I'd start with normal and go from there---it's going to be instrument dependent (in the case
of HPLC it'll be detector-dependent). Peak area is going to (usually) be positive so log-normal
would be a fine choice. 

tl;dr: logistic curve, maybe linear for qc

Long version: Most analytical instruments produce a low signal whether the analyte is
present or not but there's typically a baseline subtraction resulting in an
arbitrary quantity measured with noise when the analyte is below a minimum
detectable level.  Since you are dealing with peak area rather than signal itself
this gets subtracted out so zero means the quantitiy is less than the minimum
detectable level (assuming the pre-processing is working well). 
Then there's typically a non-linear region with increasing slope, a linear region
which is where people usually expect the instrument to be reliable for quanitfying
the analyte.  Really if you do a decent job of modeling the shape of this
curve and the uncertainty it's fine to use the non-linear region too, you'll just see
the measurement uncertainty go up as you near zero.  Finally at really
high concentrations the detector can get saturated and the response
is nonlinear again but with a decreasing slope.  With HPLC when the analyst
sees that a sample is saturating the detector (or just when they know the
concentration is high before running it) they will just dilute the sample and scale
afterwards so you may never see this issue in reported data.  If you're lucky a logistic
curve would follow this curve fine but I'm not sure if it would do a decent job
in the non-linear regions. 

In a qc situation like yours hopefully all the measurements will be right in the
middle of the linear range of the instrument (since they should know concentrations
ahead of time) and you can just use a linear relationship.

Krzysztof

 

Linas

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] hiararchical modeling in stan
parts:
Looking at your generated quantities, I don't think it makes sense to simulate
peak area (peak_area_pred).  You already observe that so if you want to add
the observational noise you could just add it directly to the measurement.  Otherwise
your are ultimately calculating the batch-level average concentration with some noise
whereas you would typically want the sample concentration and uncertainty about
it.

On Thursday, August 25, 2016 at 11:27:46 AM UTC-4, Linas Mockus wrote:
Krzysztof,

Should I use lognormal for standards? It seems the absolute error gets higher for standards with higher concentration (peak area).

I don't really think I could tell without looking at the data.  The current model assumes
a linear relationship but higher noise for higher standards might just be coming from
the instrument becoming saturated which may be a bigger problem.
I have 10 lots, 10 samples per lot, 1 injections per sample, 3 injections per standard.

I think your model makes it look like the standards are injected once per lot (?) Either that
or something is still off a little.  If so you could either make the model simpler by assuming
that the slope/intercept (c_std) are consistent across lots or get more information out of the
model by adding a hierarchical model for the slope/intercept (replacing this bit):

for (i in 1 : N_LOTS)
        c_std [i] ~ normal (0, 100);
The example is attached. I am not sure if I handle standards samples standards samples sequence most effectively. Any comments?

Thanks for sharing the example.  If you don't know the sequence I'm not sure that you could do better.  If you do know the sequence you could
use the item's position in the sequence as an effect on the baseline and response (c_std).

Krzysztof
